title: Esquites
description: Charred street-corn cups — creamy, sweet, hot, sour, in that order.

changelog.note: Created in a phone chef session — first recipe born on the go.
Cilantro now dressed per portion, never the pan — household rule.
Steps de-quantified: amounts live in the ingredient list only, so instructions stay correct at any serving scale.
Step amounts now render dynamically from the ingredient list via {id} tokens, scaling with the servings selector.

items.note: minced — seeds out for mild, in for real

steps.text: Heat {oil} in a stainless skillet over medium-high until it shimmers hard, then add {butter}, then all the corn ({corn}, kernels off) in as close to a single layer as you can manage.
steps.why: Corn is full of sugar; real contact with hot steel is what gets blackened, nutty spots instead of steamed kernels. The oil raises the butter's smoke point so it browns instead of burns.

steps.text: Leave it completely alone for 3-4 minutes. Kernels will pop and jump — that's the sign the char is happening.
steps.why: Every stir resets the browning. Char needs uninterrupted contact.

steps.text: Stir once, salt now, and char another 3 minutes.
Add {jalapeno} and {garlic}, both minced, and cook 60 seconds, just until fragrant.
steps.why: Garlic added earlier burns bitter at char temperatures. It only needs a minute to sweeten.

steps.text: Off the heat, rest 2 minutes before dressing.
steps.why: Dressing a screaming-hot pan breaks the crema and mayo to grease. Two minutes is enough.

steps.text: Fold in {crema}, {mayo}, {cotija}, and the juice of half the lime.
Taste. It should hit creamy, then sweet, then hot, then sour — in that order. Adjust lime and salt until it does.

notes.title: Why cups, not cobs
notes.body: Esquites is elote's off-the-cob sibling — dressed kernels served in a cup, eaten with a spoon. Same flavors, none of the dental commitment, and the dressing coats every kernel instead of the outside of a cob.

plating: Warm, in small glasses or cups — never a bowl; this is street food, honor it. Heavy cotija snowfall on top, a hard dust of Tajín, cilantro only on the cilantro-lovers' cups, lime wedge riding the rim.
elevations: Brown the butter before the corn goes in — 30 extra seconds and the whole cup tastes toasted.
Char the jalapeño whole in the dry pan first, then mince — smoky heat instead of sharp heat.
Tajín rim on the cups, michelada-style: wet the rim with a lime wedge, roll it in Tajín.
pairings: A cold michelada or Mexican lager
variations: No fresh corn? Frozen fire-roasted corn works — thaw, pat completely dry, and expect a little less sweetness.
